I'm not sure that it was the greatest, but certainly one of the greatest was at Windy Point Restaurant in Adelaide, Australia. Forgive the text wall, but I will just paste my review of it from the time. Read if interested, ignore otherwise; description of the food starts in the 4th paragraph.

 

The restaurant is located at the top of a hill overlooking the city and surrounding suburbs - a truly magnificent view and a new perspective on what is otherwise a rather drab city. What surprised me most about the view was how relatively flat and grid-like Adelaide is - something I appreciated about the CBD, but didn't realize held for the surrounding area.

We ate at the 20:30 sitting, which aligned with twilight, and the meal took around 2 hours (giving us the experience of dusk and night). I would absolutely recommend this sitting for anyone eating there at this time of year, as it brings out the most diversity in the cityscape and produces the most romantic ambiance. We had the best seats in the house - a table for two against the floor-to-ceiling windows at the centre of the panoramic view. I recommend the centre or just left of the centre (closer to the door) for the best view over Adelaide.

The location lived up to its name last night, with strong winds that could be heard reverberating through the roof and seen thrashing about the trees in view of the window. Around 30 minutes in, the restaurant lost power, which was unquestionably the best thing that could have happened. Without the main lighting, the city shone ever-brighter, and the restaurant was basked in the eerie but incredibly romantic light of the candles on our tables. In fact, the ambiance was so perfect, that I thought at first they had deliberately turned off the lights to improve the mood. Despite the lack of power, the restaurant still produced all meals, produced them expediently (there was only a few minutes' wait between courses - the exact amount needed for reflection and digestion), and everything was produced perfectly. I can't stress this enough... I am rather harsh when it comes to judging food; this meal was perfect.

We started with the house made olive bread, served with Woodside goat curd and tarragon oil, and the blistered truss cherry tomatoes, served with Mezcla Curado, ciabatta toast and basil aioli. The warm bread had a succulent, airy centre with crisp crust, and melted delectably in your mouth. Baked through the bread were Kalamata olives, that surprised you with bursts of saltiness and oiliness as you bit into it. The tomatoes were equally exquisite, and their accompaniment (a creamy basil aioli interlaced with syrupy balsamic vinegar) was heavenly. My only sorrow was that my palate was not sufficiently refined as to appreciate the full magnitude of the tomato dish.

For mains, I had the chateaubriand of beef, cooked blue, served with creamed spinach, and served aside with hand cut potatoes and three sauces (horseradish, Béarnaise, and what we believe was a chilli plum). I also had a side of the Black Russian tomatoes, served with buffalo mozzarella, balsamic and parsley. My companion had the house made gnocchi, with a sauce made from scorched Brussels sprouts, artichoke purée and leek. The chateaubriand was cut from Murray Valley Gold export grade grain fed eye fillet, and was equal in quality to the best I've ever eaten; succulent, mouthwatering, bursting with flavour and cooked to perfection. By the light of our iPhones, it had the most gorgeous deep burgundy colour. I didn't dare spoil it with the sauces, instead using them as dips for the potatoes - rectangular prisms of the lightest, fluffiest nature with crisp golden-brown exteriors. The chilli plum sauce (which had a name that I missed, distracted by the sensory overload of the experience), was my favourite. The portion sizes were more than generous - despite the chateaubriand being listed as 350g, it was significantly closer to 500g, and the side of Black Russian tomatoes was a meal in itself (one which I had to unfortunately send half-of back with my most profuse apologies to the chef, for I simply couldn't fit in another salivating bite without compromising the space I'd set aside for desert).

For desert we shared the chocolate mélange, which came with two servings each of mocha panna cotta, white chocolate cheesecake, hazelnut chocolate palet, butterscotch crème brûlée, chocolate mousse cornetto, and glacé cherry and chocolate parfait. You have not known decadence until you have eaten this desert. The parfait was refreshing and surprising, the crème brûlée crisp at surface with the silkiest custard underneath, but the real surprise was the palet - a viscous semi-solid melt-in-your-mouth ganache of the most satisfying rich dark chocolate. I have never previously liked deserts of this nature (I cannot stand mud cake), but this I could not only stomach, but I felt was the centrepiece of the desert platter. We accompanied our meal with a bottle of Le Mesnil Blanc de Blancs Grand Cru champagne, and Vestal sparkling water. I have never described water as "delicious" before, but this was the immediate reaction of both my companion and myself. It tasted of the purest still water, but had a perfect balance of carbonation. Le Mesnil is sourced from the same village as Krug, but has a significantly different taste. It lacks the complexities and uniqueness of the Krug taste, and lacks the oakiness of many fine champagnes, but is the creamiest champagne I have ever tasted and has a delectable long-lasting aftertaste of yeast lees, baked bread and brioche.

The restaurant is relatively inexpensive, the meal coming out at around $150 before drinks (factor in another $200 if you want to drink in style). For location, service, and, most importantly, food quality, I award Windy Point a perfect score. Simply put, it was equal to the best meals I have ever eaten, and I doubt that I will ever again come to Adelaide without eating there. 10/10
